segments.text: American history did not begin with Columbus. Beginning correctly with Indigenous societies, then explaining why different European empires colonised differently, sets up every later topic on colonial development, Indigenous removal, and continental expansion.

Indigenous peoples across North America lived in environments ranging from the Arctic to agricultural river valleys and desert regions, with political organisation ranging from small communities to complex confederacies and large settled societies — there was no single “Indian civilisation” or political system, and maize agriculture supported dense populations in many regions while other communities adapted to forest, plains or coastal economies. items.text: The transfer of crops, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and Europe/Africa following 1492.
Start with a map of Indigenous cultural regions and European claims; compare Spanish, French and English colonial objectives, settlement patterns and relations with Indigenous peoples.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “Why did English, French and Spanish colonisation take such different forms in North America?”
Do not begin American history as if no societies existed before Europeans arrived.
Do not treat Spanish, French, Dutch and English colonial systems as identical.
Do not explain Indigenous population decline only through warfare; epidemic disease was a major factor.
Indigenous societies in North America were highly diverse; there was no single political system.
Columbus’s 1492 voyage opened sustained European colonisation, disease transfer and conquest.
Jamestown, founded in 1607, became the first permanent English settlement in what became the United States.
Begin with Indigenous America on its own terms, then explain why different European empires colonised differently — never start the subject at 1492 as if nothing preceded it.
Disease-driven demographic collapse, not conquest alone, is essential to explaining the shifting balance of power in early contact.
